planting.note: Start indoors 8-10 weeks before last frost and transplant out after hardening off into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; Revolution series gerbera is bred for improved disease resistance and garden performance over florist-type gerbera.

directions: Start indoors 8-10 weeks before last frost and transplant out after hardening off into fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; Revolution series gerbera is bred for improved disease resistance and garden performance over florist-type gerbera. Large, brightly colored, daisy-like flowers in vivid shades of red, orange, yellow, pink, and white rise on sturdy stems above a low rosette of deep green, slightly fuzzy leaves, bred specifically for improved garden vigor and disease resistance compared to the more delicate gerbera varieties typically grown as cut flowers or florist pot plants. Its compact, uniform habit and strong performance in garden beds and containers, rather than just greenhouse production, have made this series a popular choice for adding bold, long-lasting color to a sunny border or patio container. Water at the base rather than overhead to reduce crown rot, deadhead spent flowers to encourage continued bloom, and treat as an annual in zones colder than 8 or a short-lived perennial in warmer climates.
sources: American Society for Horticultural Science reference

planting.note: Direct sow a few weeks before last frost into well-drained soil in full sun; Easter Bonnet sweet alyssum is a compact, heat-tolerant series that blooms earlier and holds up better in warm weather than older alyssum strains.

directions: Direct sow a few weeks before last frost into well-drained soil in full sun; Easter Bonnet sweet alyssum is a compact, heat-tolerant series that blooms earlier and holds up better in warm weather than older alyssum strains. Dense, low mounds are smothered in tiny, sweetly honey-scented flowers in shades of white, pink, rose, and purple, blooming earlier and more heat-tolerantly than older sweet alyssum strains, making it useful as an edging plant, container filler, or living mulch between vegetables where its fragrance and small size complement rather than compete with other plants. Extremely easy from seed, it self-sows readily in favorable conditions and attracts beneficial insects including hoverflies and small parasitic wasps valuable for natural pest control in a vegetable garden. Shear back by half after the first flush of bloom to encourage a fresh rebloom, and provide consistent moisture, since alyssum wilts and stops flowering in prolonged drought.

planting.note: Start indoors 6-8 weeks before last frost and transplant out after danger of frost has passed into well-drained soil in full sun; Lanai verbena is bred for improved powdery mildew resistance compared to older verbena strains.

directions: Start indoors 6-8 weeks before last frost and transplant out after danger of frost has passed into well-drained soil in full sun; Lanai verbena is bred for improved powdery mildew resistance compared to older verbena strains. Dense clusters of small, brightly colored flowers in a wide range of colors from white and pink to red, purple, and bicolor patterns cover trailing, mat-forming stems nearly continuously through the growing season, bred for improved resistance to powdery mildew, a common problem that plagued older bedding verbena varieties in humid climates. Its trailing, spreading habit and improved disease resistance make it a reliable choice for a hanging basket, container spiller, or groundcover in a sunny, well-drained bed. Water when the top inch of soil dries, avoid overhead watering which promotes fungal disease, and deadhead if seed set becomes heavy to encourage continued bloom.
sources: American Society for Horticultural Science reference

planting.note: Start indoors 8-10 weeks before last frost and transplant out after danger of frost has passed into well-drained soil in full sun; Serena angelonia is a compact, seed-grown series that flowers reliably through Gulf South summer heat.

directions: Start indoors 8-10 weeks before last frost and transplant out after danger of frost has passed into well-drained soil in full sun; Serena angelonia is a compact, seed-grown series that flowers reliably through Gulf South summer heat. Spikes of small, orchid-like flowers in shades of purple, pink, white, and lavender rise above narrow, glossy foliage on a compact, well-branched plant that blooms continuously through the hottest, most humid part of summer without deadheading, making it one of the most heat- and humidity-tolerant bedding annuals available for a Gulf South garden. Its compact, uniform, seed-grown habit and outstanding summer heat performance have made it a mainstay of commercial and home landscaping across the warm-summer South, holding color and form when many other bedding annuals falter in extreme heat. Water when the top inch of soil dries, and expect vigorous, low-maintenance bloom through the entire summer without deadheading.
sources: American Society for Horticultural Science reference

planting.note: Plant transplants after last frost into well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; Breathless euphorbia is a compact, mounding selection bred for a fuller, denser habit than the similar Diamond Frost cultivar.

directions: Plant transplants after last frost into well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; Breathless euphorbia is a compact, mounding selection bred for a fuller, denser habit than the similar Diamond Frost cultivar. Countless tiny, star-shaped white flowers cover a dense, airy mound of fine-textured foliage nearly continuously through the growing season, creating a soft, baby's-breath-like cloud of white that serves as an excellent filler between bolder, more colorful companions in a mixed container or border. More compact and densely mounding than the popular Diamond Frost cultivar, it needs little deadheading or maintenance to maintain its nonstop flower display through summer heat and humidity. Water when the top inch of soil dries, avoid overwatering which can lead to root rot, and note that the milky sap can irritate skin, so wear gloves when handling or pruning.
sources: American Society for Horticultural Science reference
